newsitem.title: USA: Florida sheriff defends comments on tourism.
newsitem.headline: Florida sheriff defends comments on tourism.

text.p: Four days after he said the state was too dangerous to visit, a Florida sheriff combed the halls of the capitol Tuesday defending his comments and saying Florida needs to do something about violent crime.

Lee County Sheriff John McDougall, who Friday told viewers of NBC's "Today" show to stay away from Florida because of its high crime rate and the recent release of hundreds of prison inmates, said he wanted a constitutional amendment to keep prisoners locked up longer.
"I didn't say what I said to cause controversy," McDougall told Reuters. "I said what I said because it was a true statement. Nonetheless it became controversial.
His comments made news not only in the United States but in Europe, where fear of crime following several high-profile murders of tourists several years ago cut the number of visitors to the state.
Nine European tourists were murdered in Florida during a 12-month period in 1992-93, damaging the crucial $38 billion-a-year industry.

McDougall met Tuesday with several lawmakers, but was unable to meet Gov. Lawton Chiles or Attorney General Bob Butterworth. Florida Sen. Charlie Crist, a St. Petersburg Republican, defended McDougall's comments and thanked him for his perseverance.
"He expressed a concern about the crime problem in Florida," Crist said. "The man happens to be right. Hello, watch the news at night or read the newspaper in the morning. It's a problem."

Crist was the Senate sponsor of the 1995 Stop Turning Out Prisoners Act, which now requires inmates to serve 85 percent of their sentences. The law, however, only affects those convicted and sentenced after that date.

By contrast, tens of thousands of inmates sentenced in the late 1980s and early 1990s were the beneficiaries of generous reductions in their sentences to ease overcrowding in state prisons. In some cases, prisoners were serving less than 33 percent of their sentences.

McDougall's comments were sparked by the release of 500 rapists, murderers, kidnappers and other violent offenders in the past two weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a 1996 state edict aimed at keeping them in prison longer.
